levels.title: Facts and Moves
levels.story: At the dock, Rowan hands Kit two parcels. Parcel p must go to the Dock and parcel q must come back to the Cabin. "Write the world as a list of facts," says Rowan. "Then every move is: what must be true, what becomes true, what stops being true."

everyday.scene: A recipe says what you need before a step, such as flour on the bench, and what is different afterwards: dough made, flour used. STRIPS writes actions down in the same way.
everyday.question: How can a computer be told what each action does?
everyday.answer: It is told what facts must be true first, which facts the action makes true, and which it makes false.

lessons.title: A world of facts
text: STRIPS describes a world as a set of facts that are true right now. Anything not listed is taken to be false. Kit's world has facts like 'Kit at Cabin', 'p at Cabin' and 'q at Dock'.
The goal is a set of facts too: 'p at Dock' and 'q at Cabin'. A state is a goal state when it contains every goal fact. Facts such as 'Kit has p' describe the parcel being carried.

terms.meaning: A statement that is true in the current state.
The set of facts that are true right now.

lessons.title: Three lists per action
text: Each action has three lists. Its preconditions are the facts that must already be true. Its add list holds the facts that become true. Its delete list holds the facts that stop being true.
The new state is the old state, minus the delete list, plus the add list. Take 'pick p at Cabin'. It needs Kit at Cabin and p at Cabin, adds Kit has p, and deletes p at Cabin.

terms.meaning: A fact that must be true before the action can run.
Facts that stop being true afterwards.

lessons.title: A plan is a path through states
text: A plan is a list of actions where each one's preconditions are true when its turn comes, and the last state contains every goal fact. Kit's shortest plan for the two parcels has 8 actions.

Kit can stand in 3 places, and each parcel can be at one of 3 places or in Kit's hands. That makes 3 x 4 x 4 = 48 different states, and all 48 can be reached. Searching them blindly is slow, which is why the next levels add guidance.

deeper.title: Blocks world
text: Planning researchers often use a 'blocks world', with blocks stacked on a table, to test ideas. Kit's parcels play the same role: a small world that shows how facts, actions and plans fit together.

fieldNotes.title: STRIPS
fieldNotes.text: STRIPS was developed by Richard Fikes and Nils Nilsson in 1971 at SRI International. Its way of writing problems is the base for most planning languages used today.

fieldNotes.title: Actions in STRIPS
fieldNotes.text: Each STRIPS action lists what must be true before it runs and what it makes true and false afterwards.

fieldNotes.title: Blocks world
fieldNotes.text: The blocks world is a planning domain from artificial intelligence research, and it is a standard example of a toy problem: a simple setting for testing ideas.

summary: You described a world as a set of facts, wrote actions with preconditions, an add list and a delete list, and followed an 8-action plan through the states.
Rowan checks the list. "Every move written down, nothing hidden." Kit nods. "Now I can hand this to a program, if I write it in its language."

mistake.title: Forgetting the delete list
mistake.text: An action that only adds facts leaves old ones behind, so Kit would stand at the Cabin and the Bridge at once. The delete list removes what is no longer true.

levels.title: Write the Domain
levels.story: Rowan pins two sheets of paper to a tree. "This one says how any delivery world works," says Rowan. "This one says what is in the wood today." Kit reads them side by side. "The rules, and the setup."

everyday.scene: A board game has a rule book that works for every game you play, and a setup card that shows where the pieces start today.
everyday.question: How do you write a planning problem so that any planner can read it?
everyday.answer: You split it into a domain, the rules of the world, and a problem, today's objects, starting facts and goal, written in a shared language such as PDDL.

lessons.title: Two files
text: PDDL, the Planning Domain Definition Language, writes a planning task as two files. The domain file holds what stays the same: the kinds of facts and the actions. The problem file holds one situation: the objects, the starting facts and the goal.
Think of a board game. The rule book works for every game, and the setup card shows where the pieces start today. Many planners read PDDL, so one description can be handed to different planners.

terms.meaning: The rules: facts and actions that work for any problem in this kind of world.
One situation: objects, starting facts and goal.

lessons.title: Reading an action
text: A PDDL action has a name, parameters, a precondition and an effect. A word that starts with a question mark, like ?from, is a variable that gets filled in. In the effect, a plain fact is added and a fact wrapped in not is deleted.
Our move action needs a road between the two places and Kit at the starting place. The facts about roads never change, but writing them as preconditions keeps meaningless moves from ever running.

head: Line of the domain file
What it says
rows: Two blanks to fill with places
Needs a road, and Kit at the starting place
Adds Kit at the new place, deletes Kit at the old one

lessons.title: The problem file
text: The problem file names its domain, lists the objects that exist today, gives the facts that are true at the start, and states the goal. Change the objects, facts or goal, and you have a new problem in the same world.
Adding a third parcel r would change only this file, because the domain's pick and drop actions work for any parcel.

head: Line of the problem file
What it says
rows: (:init (kit-at cabin) (at p cabin) (at q dock) (road cabin bridge) ...)
Facts the plan must make true

fieldNotes.title: PDDL
fieldNotes.text: PDDL is an attempt to standardise AI planning languages. It was first developed by Drew McDermott and colleagues in 1998 for the International Planning Competition.

fieldNotes.title: Domain and problem
fieldNotes.text: PDDL describes a domain, with its actions, and a problem that gives a concrete instance. The planner produces a sequence of actions as output.

fieldNotes.title: From STRIPS to PDDL
fieldNotes.text: STRIPS was the base for most of the languages used to express planning problems today, PDDL among them.

summary: You split a task into a domain file and a problem file, read a move action line by line, watched its blanks get filled in, and saw what the problem file adds.
Rowan hangs the sheets on a hook. "Now any planner can pick them up." Kit rings the bell. "Even one I have never met."

mistake.title: Mixing up the two files
mistake.text: Rules that work everywhere belong in the domain. Anything that describes one situation, like the goal, belongs in the problem.
